headline: AI Agents Get Physical Hands with new PAL open standard
summary: A freshman's proposal for an open standard that allows AI agents to directly control hardware, bypassing complex frameworks.
details: AI agents can already write code, browse the web, and manage servers, but they lack the ability to interact with the physical world. This new proposal, PAL (Physical Abstraction Layer), aims to change that by enabling AI agents to control hardware directly.

The core idea is to leverage the Python REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) as the simplest form of Inter-Process Communication (IPC). This approach avoids the need for complex tool registries or JSON schemas, allowing agents to send Python code directly to hardware.

PAL utilizes a dual-core architecture on microcontrollers. Core 0, written in C, acts as a stable foundation that never changes, handling critical functions like a watchdog timer. Core 1, running MicroPython, serves as the agent's playground, executing commands received over WebSocket with low latency.

This architecture ensures determinism and stability for physical control while allowing the AI agent the flexibility it needs for reasoning and iteration. The system is designed to be robust, with Core 0 automatically restarting Core 1 if the agent misbehaves or crashes.

The reference implementation is currently under development for the ESP32-S3, but the specification is designed to be hardware-agnostic. A single cloud-based AI agent can manage numerous PAL terminals across various devices, offering a scalable solution.

The proposal emphasizes that AI agents don't need to be smarter; they need to be idempotent and capable of interacting with the real world. PAL provides a standardized way for them to gain these physical 'hands'.
The PAL specification is currently at version 0.1, and the developer, a freshman at Anhui University of Science and Technology, is seeking community input and collaboration.

headline_marked: [[Mirage app]] streams your Mac display to iPhone, iPad, and Vision Pro
headline: Mirage app streams your Mac display to iPhone, iPad, and Vision Pro
summary: A new indie app allows users to extend their Mac's desktop to other Apple devices, including the Vision Pro headset.
details: The new app, called Mirage, enables users to stream their Mac's display to an iPhone, iPad, or even the Apple Vision Pro headset.
This allows for a seamless extension of the Mac workspace across multiple devices, offering increased flexibility for productivity and multitasking.
Mirage is developed by an indie developer and aims to provide a powerful yet simple solution for users who want to leverage their existing Apple hardware in new ways.
The app supports streaming to other Macs as well, effectively turning them into secondary displays for your primary Mac.
While specific performance metrics and pricing details are not yet widely available, the app is positioned as a tool for developers and power users looking to enhance their workflow.
